I. The Trump administration has imposed fresh sanctions on Russia as punitive measures
relating to Moscow’s refusal to strike a ceasefire agreement to bring the war in Ukraine to a
halt, with Washington targeting Russian oil giants Rosneft and Lukoil. Russia’s use of the oil
trade to finance war has been a bone of contention for NATO members since the early days of
Russia’s incursion into and attacks on Ukraine, an indirect dimension of the conflict that has
pulled Asian powers India and China into the fray. Over the summer, Mr. Trump sought to up
the ante in this regard by slapping India with an additional 25% tariff for importing Russian
oil, over and above the basic 25% rate imposed on other countries as well, even though China,
as a top importer of Russian seaborne crude, was spared this levy. Now, the latest round of
sanctions appeared to have penalised both trading partners of Moscow significantly, with
reports suggesting that at least four major state-owned Chinese oil companies have suspended
purchases from Russia and that at least one private and three state-owned Indian refinery
companies are planning for “recalibration of Russian oil imports” including the possibility of
a “massive cut” over time.
At the heart of the White House move is the seething frustration of Mr. Trump over failed
attempts to not only bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table — a feat
achieved in Alaska in August and a second summit agreed in Budapest before it was postponed
following the collapse of ceasefire talks — but also to nudge the Kremlin towards at least a
short-term arrangement that might lead to a cessation of hostilities as a precursor to a broader
treaty on territorial and institutional agreements. It is possible that the latest sanctions may lead
to a genuine tightening of options for Mr. Putin on ending the war, especially as Washington
will now be joining the European Union that has adopted its 19th sanctions package against
Moscow, specifically focusing on technology supply chains, energy revenues, and financial
networks. Nevertheless, it may be premature to applaud their potential impact on the Kremlin’s
strategic calculus. Ultimately, whether sanctions have teeth or not depends on the consistency
of their enforcement, including shutting down the inevitable loopholes and workarounds that
Moscow will seek to exploit to continue selling oil abroad, possibly at even sharper discounts.
Mr. Trump may find that he has travelled full circle to arrive at the same sticky negotiating
points between Moscow and Kiev that his predecessor faced — an early end to ground
hostilities, control of Donbas, and the permissible extent of NATO influence in the region. Only
if sanctions can break Russian strategic will on at least one of these points will the prospects
for                        peace                        brighten                         considerably.

questions.stimulus:
II. Nikolay Tchikildyeev, a waiter in the Moscow hotel, Slavyansky Bazaar, was taken ill. His
legs went numb and his gait was affected, so that on one occasion, as he was going along the
corridor, he tumbled and fell down with a tray full of ham and peas. He had to leave his job.
All his own savings and his wife's were spent on doctors and medicines; they had nothing left
to live upon. He felt dull with no work to do, and he made up his mind he must go home to the
village. It is better to be ill at home, and living there is cheaper; and it is a true saying that the
walls of home are a help.
He reached Zhukovo towards evening. In his memories of childhood he had pictured his home
as bright, snug, comfortable. Now, going into the hut, he was positively frightened; it was so
dark, so crowded, so unclean. His wife Olga and his daughter Sasha, who had come with him,
kept looking in bewilderment at the big untidy stove, which filled up almost half the hut and
was black with soot and flies. What lots of flies! The stove was on one side, the beams lay
slanting on the walls, and it looked as though the hut were just going to fall to pieces. In the
corner, facing the door, under the holy images, bottle labels and newspaper cuttings were stuck
on the walls instead of pictures. The poverty, the poverty!
Of the grown-up people there were none at home; all were at work at the harvest. On the stove
was sitting a white-headed girl of eight, unwashed and apathetic; she did not even glance at
them as they came in. On the floor a white cat was rubbing itself against the oven fork.
"Puss, puss!" Sasha called to her. "Puss!"
"She can't hear," said the little girl; "she has gone deaf."
"How is that?"
"Oh, she was beaten."


Nikolay and Olga realized from the first glance what life was like here, but said nothing to one
another; in silence they put down their bundles, and went out into the village street. Their hut
was the third from the end, and seemed the very poorest and oldest-looking; the second was
not much better; but the last one had an iron roof, and curtains in the windows. That hut stood
apart, not enclosed; it was a tavern. The huts were in a single row, and the whole of the little
village -- quiet and dreamy, with willows, elders, and mountain-ash trees peeping out from the
yards -- had an attractive look.

V. WHAT DO women really carry around in their just-in-case purse: lipstick, pepper spray, two
snacks, a tampon, three tissues… If Mary Poppins were Indian, she would be every woman
with a tote bag. Unlike the men in their lives, whose pockets hold, maybe, a phone and a wallet,
women’s purses carry universes inside them. The bags aren’t simply accessories; they are
portable archives of responsibility, preparedness and a little bit of magic.
The insides of a purse may seem like clutter, but it isn’t. It’s a labour of love, fear and foresight
translated into objects. Each just-in-case item is a woman’s way of carrying not just herself,
but everyone she cares about. But why do women do this? Because they are conditioned to live
in the land of just-in-case. Just in case someone falls sick, just in case a child cries, just in case
the car breaks down. The purse is less about fashion and more about forethought. An invisible
syllabus of caregiving tucked into zippers.
From a psychological lens, the just-in-case purse isn’t about objects; it reflects the mental load
women carry every day. Research shows that women are often socialised into anticipatory
caregiving; they not only respond to needs, but also predict them. The Band-Aid is for the
scrapes that haven’t happened yet, the snacks for a hunger no one has admitted to yet and the
tissues for tears not yet cried.
Entire industries thrive on the idea that women must always be prepared. Cosmetics, fashion
and lifestyle brands have mastered the art of packaging responsibility into something portable.
The travel perfume that promises confidence, the compact powder that claims to save face, the
foldable flats marketed as a rescue from heels that betray you at midnight. None of these are
sold as luxuries. They are sold as safeguards. Preparedness becomes something that can be
purchased, wrapped in glossy packaging, and tucked neatly into a handbag. This expectation
turns resilience into a market. What looks like empowerment is often pressure in disguise,
urging women to buy not just products, but a sense of peace of mind. The just-in-case purse,
then, is not simply about habit or preference. It is a cultural construct, shaped as much by
advertising as by tradition, tying identity to preparedness and responsibility to consumption

V. In a move that challenges the very spirit of free inquiry, Government of India (GoI) has
asked ministries to revisit how PhD guides are chosen and to steer doctoral research toward
innovation, national priorities and stronger academia—industry collaboration. While closer ties
with industry are desirable, the zealous drive to accelerate R&D— from dictating who can
guide to what may be researched—risks stifling academic freedom.
For a country racing to catch up in the global innovation sweepstakes, the temptation to direct
research toward state-declared priorities is understandable. After all, central planning of
research yielded visible results in China and the erstwhile Soviet Union. But those models came
with a heavy cost—narrowing the field of enquiry, silencing unconventional thought, and often
discouraging the very curiosity that fuels genuine discovery. No matter how well-intentioned,
a ‘helping hand’ that steers too tightly ends up throttling what it seeks to nurture.
A state-approved list of research themes or mentors would push aside ‘non-priority’ areas —
the arts, humanities, and blue-sky sciences that often yield breakthroughs because they wander
off the beaten path. Innovation rarely flourishes under supervision. It thrives in the freely
explored, where failure is tolerated and curiosity unrestrained. Academic freedom is not an
indulgence; it is the oxygen of progress and the foundation on which great nations build their
scientific and cultural capital. India’s challenge is to find that balance between guiding research
and granting freedom. GoI should identify national priorities and channel more incentives
toward them. But that must come as an invitation, not an instruction. The record worldwide is
clear: chokeholds on research do not produce results — freedom, diversity, and a culture that
celebrates                                      questioning                                     do.

IX. Sentencing and punishment under the Indian Penal Code, 1860, form the cornerstone of
India’s retributive and reformative criminal justice system. Section 53 of the IPC enumerates
the permissible punishments, creating a hierarchical and discretionary framework for courts to
impose penalties commensurate with the gravity of the offence. The types of punishments
include Death Penalty, Life Imprisonment, Imprisonment (which may be rigorous or simple),
Forfeiture of Property, and Fine. These sanctions are not mutually exclusive; often, fines are
imposed in conjunction with imprisonment.
The most severe sanction, the death penalty, is reserved for the “rarest of rare” cases, a doctrinal
limitation crafted by the Supreme Court in the landmark case of Bachan Singh v. State of
Punjab (1980). This doctrine mandates that capital punishment is an exception, not the rule, to
be invoked only when the alternative of life imprisonment is “unquestionably foreclosed.” The
court must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances of the crime and the criminal,
ensuring the sentence is proportionate. Its application is typically confined to certain forms of
aggravated murder and terrorism-related offences. The procedure is also meticulously
safeguarded, requiring confirmation by a High Court and affording the convict multiple
avenues of appeal and mercy petitions.
Life imprisonment, often misunderstood as incarceration for a precise term, generally means
imprisonment for the remainder of the convict’s natural life, though remissions and parole
mechanisms exist. Imprisonment is bifurcated into rigorous and simple. Rigorous
imprisonment involves compulsory hard labour, while simple imprisonment entails
confinement without such labour, prescribed for less severe offences. Forfeiture of property, a
consequential penalty, involves the confiscation of assets and is sometimes specified for certain
crimes against the state. Lastly, a fine can be a sole punishment or a supplementary one, with
the court possessing the power to impose imprisonment in default of its payment, subject to
statutory limits.
Thus, the IPC provides a structured yet flexible sentencing palette, ranging from the ultimate
sanction of death to pecuniary penalties, guided by principles of proportionality,
individualization, and, in the context of capital punishment, an exceedingly high threshold of
judicial scrutiny. The system continually negotiates the tensions between societal demand for
retribution and the constitutional values of justice and human dignity.

X. Within the intricate framework of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, several equitable
doctrines operate to ensure justice, clarity, and the effective administration of property rights.
Among these, the Rule Against Perpetuity, the Doctrine of Election, and the Doctrine of Merger
serve as foundational pillars, while the related Doctrine of Cy-pres governs charitable trusts.


The Rule Against Perpetuity, encapsulated in Section 14, is a central pillar of property law
designed to prevent the tying up of property inalienably for an excessive period. It mandates
that no future interest in property is valid unless it must vest, if at all, within a life or lives in
being at the creation of the interest plus twenty-one years, excluding the period of gestation.
This rule strikes a crucial balance between allowing settlors to control the future devolution of
their assets and ensuring that property remains marketable and free from dead-hand control for
generations, thereby serving the public interest by facilitating its circulation in the economy.


The Doctrine of Election, detailed in Section 35, embodies the equitable maxim that one cannot
approbate and reprobate. It stipulates that if an instrument, such as a will or deed, purports to
transfer a property belonging to another person while also conferring a benefit on that same
person, the beneficiary must choose (elect) either to accept the benefit under the instrument,
thereby surrendering their own property, or to retain their own property, forfeiting the conferred
benefit. This doctrine ensures fairness by preventing a person from taking advantage of an
instrument while simultaneously disregarding its dispositive provisions.
Distinct from election, the Doctrine of Merger addresses the confluence of estates. It operates
automatically when a lesser estate and a greater estate in the same property unite in the same
person, in the same right, with no intermediate interest existing between them. For instance, if
a lessee acquires the freehold (ownership) of the leased property, the leasehold interest merges
into the freehold and extinguishes. The intent of the parties may sometimes prevent merger, but
the doctrine's primary purpose is to simplify the title by eliminating superfluous and coexisting
interests held by a single individual.
While the Doctrine of Cy-pres finds its statutory home in the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, it is
conceptually vital in property law concerning charitable trusts. It empowers the court, when
the specific purpose of a charitable trust becomes impossible or impracticable to fulfil, to direct
the trust property to be applied cy-pres (as near as possible) to the original general charitable
intent of the settlor. This prevents the failure of the trust and ensures that charitable resources
continue to serve the public good, adapting to changing circumstances without violating the
settlor’s core philanthropic vision.
Together, these doctrines create a harmonious system that balances individual autonomy in
property disposition with overarching principles of fairness, alienability, and the public interest.

XI. The discharge of a contract signifies the termination of the contractual relationship between
the parties, extinguishing their respective rights and obligations. The Indian Contract Act, 1872,
provides several distinct modes through which a contract can be legally discharged, moving
beyond mere completion.
The most ideal and frequent mode is discharge by performance (Section 37), where both parties
fulfil their promises precisely as per the terms. The contract is said to be discharged when the
obligations are executed, leaving no outstanding duties. Performance must be complete,
precise, and by the promisor or their authorised agent to be effective.
Parties may also mutually agree to end or modify their agreement. Discharge by agreement or
consent is facilitated under Sections 62 and 63. This encompasses novation, where an existing
contract is substituted with a new one involving either the same or new parties; rescission,
which involves the mutual abandonment of all contractual obligations; alteration, where one or
more terms are modified by mutual consent; and remission, where a promisee accepts a lesser
fulfilment than what was originally promised.
A contract may be discharged under the doctrine of frustration (Section 56), which deals with
subsequent impossibility or unlawfulness. If an event, unforeseen at the time of contracting and
not due to either party's fault, renders the performance impossible or radically different from
what was envisaged, the contract becomes void. Examples include destruction of the subject
matter, a change in law making performance illegal, or the death or incapacity of a person
crucial for performance. The core is the occurrence of a subsequent, unavoidable change in
circumstances.
Finally, discharge by breach (Section 39) occurs when one party fails to perform their
obligation. Breach can be actual, upon the failure to perform on the due date, or anticipatory,
where a party repudiates the contract before the performance is due. In an anticipatory breach,
the aggrieved party is immediately entitled to sue for damages without waiting for the actual
performance date. A breach, whether actual or anticipatory, does not automatically terminate
the contract; it gives the injured party the option to treat the contract as rescinded and claim
compensation, thereby discharging their own future obligations.
Thus, the Act provides a comprehensive framework, recognising that contractual bonds can
dissolve not only through successful execution but also through mutual accord, unforeseen
impossibility, or the failure of a party to uphold their promise.

XII. The constitutional mechanism for evolving India's official language policy is a carefully
crafted procedural compromise, established under Article 344 of the Constitution. This
provision mandates the President to constitute an Official Language Commission at the
expiration of ten years from the Constitution's commencement, and thereafter as deemed
necessary. However, the President's authority in appointing this Commission is not absolute. A
critical proviso to Clause (1) imposes a specific linguistic balance, requiring that the
Commission consist of members drawn in equal proportion from both the Hindi-speaking and
the non-Hindi-speaking states. This structural safeguard ensures regional and linguistic equity


in a body whose recommendations could significantly impact the Union's administrative
language.
The Commission's primary duty is to make recommendations to the President on the
progressive use of Hindi, the restrictions on English, and related matters. Its report, however,
does not take direct effect. It enters a unique deliberative phase where a Committee of
Parliament, comprising thirty members from the Lok Sabha and twenty from the Rajya Sabha,
scrutinizes it. The primary constitutional function of this Parliamentary Committee is to act as
a vital political filter, providing its own views and recommendations for the President's
consideration alongside the Commission's report. This creates a dialogic process between
expert recommendation and political consensus.
Following this, the President may issue a directive based on the Commission's
recommendations and the Committee's report. Crucially, Article 344(4) clarifies the nature of
this directive: it is expressly non-justiciable, and its implementation is left entirely to the
discretion of Parliament. This process inherently acknowledges a potential constitutional
tension. Recommendations to restrict English could impact civil servants from non-Hindi
regions, potentially engaging the fundamental right to equality of opportunity in matters of
public employment under Article 16, as language proficiency could become an unreasonable
barrier.
Historically, the first Official Language Commission (1955), chaired by B.G. Kher, played a
foundational role. While operating within its constitutional terms, it made an influential
recommendation that transcended its immediate mandate and became a cornerstone of national
policy: the adoption of a three-language formula in school education. This proposal aimed to
balance the promotion of Hindi, the continued use of English, and the study of a modern Indian
language, thereby embodying the pluralistic spirit of India's language policy framework.

XIII. In its landmark ruling upholding Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, the Supreme Court's
majority opinion employed the Preambular value of "Fraternity" as a decisive constitutional
anchor. This rationale served to implicitly reject a significant alternative challenge: that the
provision was arbitrary for creating a special citizenship rule only for Assam, thereby violating
Article 14's guarantee of equality. The Court reasoned that the unique historical context of
migration into Assam, culminating in the Assam Accord, justified a differentiated legal
response to foster national unity and integration, thus satisfying the test of reasonable
classification under Article 14.
This conclusion was not unanimous. The dissenting opinion issued a profound caution, arguing
that accepting the petitioners’ claim of a demographic threat to cultural identity could establish
a dangerous precedent. This warning is best understood as an alert against legitimizing internal
discrimination based on origin, akin to creating "insiders" and "outsiders" within a state, which
could undermine the constitutional framework of a unified citizenship.
Acknowledging serious flaws in implementation, the majority issued a singular directive for
the Chief Justice of India to constitute a monitoring Bench. This extraordinary procedural
measure most closely aligns with the Court's strategic use of its power to exercise continuing
mandamus to ensure executive compliance with laws, a tool used to oversee complex, long-
term enforcement where governmental inaction has been chronic.
On the substantive question of cultural rights, the judgment clarified that the protection for any
section of citizens to conserve their distinct culture under Article 29(1) operates irrespective of
demographic change. This legal interpretation implies that this fundamental right is primarily
a guarantee against state action that actively destroys or prohibits the culture, not a shield
against demographic shifts resulting from lawful migration or political processes.
Ultimately, the Court emphasized that the petitioners failed to prove that Section 6A itself
compromised the Assamese people's cultural safeguards. This underscores a foundational
principle of constitutional litigation: a law is presumed valid, and the burden rests on the
challenger to demonstrate it is manifestly arbitrary or bears no reasonable nexus to a legitimate
state aim. The petitioners' inability to discharge this burden was central to the provision's
survival.

questions.stimulus:
XIV. International law demonstrates its capacity for profound impact through specialized
treaties that address distinct global challenges. Two exemplary agreements, originating in
different decades and targeting vastly different threats, stand out for their successful,
convention-based approach: the Mine Ban Treaty and the Montreal Protocol.


The Mine Ban Treaty, formally known as the Ottawa Treaty, represents a landmark in
humanitarian disarmament law. It was driven by a coalition of states, civil society, and
international organizations horrified by the indiscriminate and lingering impact of anti-
personnel landmines on civilians, long after conflicts have ended. The treaty’s core obligations
are unequivocal: it prohibits the use, stockpiling, production, and transfer of anti-personnel
mines. It also mandates the clearance of mined areas and assistance for victims. By establishing
a clear norm against these weapons, the Ottawa Treaty has created a powerful stigma, leading
to a dramatic reduction in their use and the destruction of millions of stockpiled mines, saving
countless lives and limbs.
In the environmental sphere, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone
Layer is heralded as one of the most successful international treaties ever crafted. Confronted
with compelling scientific evidence that man-made chemicals were eroding the Earth’s
protective ozone layer, the international community acted decisively. The treaty is designed to
protect the ozone layer by phasing out the production and consumption of Ozone Depleting
Substances, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons. Its innovative framework includes
binding phase-out schedules for developed and developing countries, a financial mechanism to
aid compliance, and a scientific assessment panel to guide its evolution. This adaptable,
science-based regime has led to the near-elimination of major ozone-depleting chemicals,
allowing the ozone layer to begin a slow recovery and providing a crucial model for multilateral
environmental cooperation.
Together, these treaties illustrate how focused legal instruments, built on scientific evidence or
humanitarian imperative and supported by robust implementation mechanisms, can deliver
tangible, life-preserving results for humanity and the planet.

XIV. International law demonstrates its capacity for profound impact through specialized
treaties that address distinct global challenges. Two exemplary agreements, originating in
different decades and targeting vastly different threats, stand out for their successful,
convention-based approach: the Mine Ban Treaty and the Montreal Protocol.

humanitarian disarmament law. It was driven by a coalition of states, civil society, and
international organizations horrified by the indiscriminate and lingering impact of anti-
personnel landmines on civilians, long after conflicts have ended. The treaty’s core obligations
are unequivocal: it prohibits the use, stockpiling, production, and transfer of anti-personnel
mines. It also mandates the clearance of mined areas and assistance for victims. By establishing
a clear norm against these weapons, the Ottawa Treaty has created a powerful stigma, leading
to a dramatic reduction in their use and the destruction of millions of stockpiled mines, saving
countless lives and limbs.
In the environmental sphere, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone
Layer is heralded as one of the most successful international treaties ever crafted. Confronted
with compelling scientific evidence that man-made chemicals were eroding the Earth’s
protective ozone layer, the international community acted decisively. The treaty is designed to
protect the ozone layer by phasing out the production and consumption of Ozone Depleting
Substances, such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons. Its innovative framework includes
binding phase-out schedules for developed and developing countries, a financial mechanism to
aid compliance, and a scientific assessment panel to guide its evolution. This adaptable,
science-based regime has led to the near-elimination of major ozone-depleting chemicals,
allowing the ozone layer to begin a slow recovery and providing a crucial model for multilateral
environmental cooperation.

humanitarian imperative and supported by robust implementation mechanisms, can deliver
tangible, life-preserving results for humanity and the planet.

questions.stimulus:
XVI. Imagine you are in charge of India's money. Your main job is to keep prices stable. Your
main tool is the repo rate, which is the interest rate at which you lend money to banks. When
you change this rate, it eventually changes the cost of every loan in the country, from big factory
loans to your family's car EMI. Recently, the RBI had a big meeting and kept the repo rate
unchanged at 5.25 per cent. On the surface, this looks like doing nothing. But in finance,
choosing to do nothing can be a powerful decision. Let us understand why.


The RBI watches two big things: inflation, which means how much prices rise, and growth,
which means how fast the economy expands. Ideally, inflation should be around 4 per cent.
Right now, inflation has fallen sharply to around 2-2.5 per cent, which is well below the target.
At the same time, the economy is still growing. So a simple textbook would say this is the
perfect moment to cut rates, because lower rates make loans cheaper and encourage spending.
So why did the RBI not cut?


The answer is that the RBI knows real life is more complicated. It looks at the story behind the
numbers. The first reason is that not all inflation drops are permanent. Inflation fell mainly
because food prices dropped. This is good news, but also tricky. In India, food prices go up and
down a lot. A drop might not last. If next year's monsoon is bad, food prices could shoot right
back up. If the RBI cuts rates now because of temporarily low food prices, it could backfire.
Cheaper loans would put more money in people's pockets. If food prices then rise again, people
will have more money to spend on expensive food, making inflation even worse. So the RBI
is waiting to see if this low inflation is here to stay or just a temporary visitor.


The second reason is that past decisions take time to work. Imagine watering a garden with a
long hose. When you turn the tap, water takes time to reach the plants. Similarly, when the RBI
cuts rates, it takes time for the effect to reach you through cheaper bank loans and lower EMIs.
The RBI has already cut rates significantly over the past year. That water is still flowing through
the system. If they cut again before the first cuts have fully worked, they might overwater the
garden and cause problems later. So when the RBI keeps rates on hold, it is not ignoring the
economy. It is being patient, watching carefully, and waiting to see what happens next.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “RBI is buying time by not cutting the repo rate. Past
policy needs a breather to work”, ThePrint.]

XVII. What makes human beings unique? Throughout history, we’ve given this quality many
names—the human spirit, the human condition, or the soul. Some have tried to explain it away,
arguing we’re just another animal. Others have called it divine, beyond explanation.


Today, this debate is heating up again. Artificial intelligence—specifically large language
models like ChatGPT—is challenging our assumptions about what makes us special. When
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, tweeted “i am a stochastic parrot, and so r u,” he was responding
to linguist Emily Bender’s claim that these systems merely spit out predictable words without
real understanding. One side argues machines can never truly be like us. The other suggests the
differences aren’t so clear.


This isn’t the first time technology has sparked such conflict. During the Industrial Revolution,
society faced a similar divide. On one side were rationalists who saw human behaviour as
something to be measured, managed and optimised like a machine. On the other were
Romantics who defended subjective feeling, individual genius and the organic nature of human
life against the spread of mechanism.


Today, AI is reigniting this war across multiple fronts—science, art and politics. Can machines
truly be creative? Can they make ethical judgments? Or will there always remain something
essentially human that technology cannot capture?


To answer these questions, we need to look at three key areas: knowledge, beauty and morality.
In each domain, humans demonstrate capacities that may elude computation—wisdom in how
we apply knowledge, creativity in how we imagine new possibilities, and autonomy in how we
make moral choices.


The philosophers Immanuel Kant and G W F Hegel pointed to freedom as the core of human
uniqueness. But this freedom isn’t simple. It combines our ability to pursue truth, create beauty
and choose what’s right. Understanding these elements might help us not only appreciate our
own humanity but perhaps one day build machines that share in these pursuits.


Could we create artificial souls? The question is no longer just philosophical. It’s becoming
urgent.


[Extracted with revisions and edits from “Geist in the machine”, aeon.]
